assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, built on Katori's magic-wavelength idea and Ye's realisation of extreme coherence and systematic control, give fractional uncertainties near 1e-18. That is a qualitative advance in precision measurement, and it opens tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy and a redefinition of the second. It is atomic physics at its best: a clear conceptual invention, followed by precision that other laboratories reproduce.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice and made the early demonstrations. Ye's JILA group brought the clock to the highest accuracy and stability. A two-person prize fits. Others, such as Lemonde, Hinkley and Ludlow, were important in specific milestones, but the decisive invention and its first realisation are covered by these two. Hall and Hänsch were recognised in 2005 for the comb.
assessment.maturity: Mature: many independent clocks (Sr, Yb, Hg) in several countries agree at the 1e-18 level and are used in international comparisons. Timing is good, given the roughly two decades since the 2003 proposal and 2005-2008 demonstrations.
uncertainties: How the committee weighs this against the already recognised ion clocks (Wineland 2012) and combs (2005).
Whether relative credit for early Sr lattice demonstrations among groups, including Lemonde's, should be reflected.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cold atoms in optical lattices realise Hubbard-type many-body models with a clean, tunable Hamiltonian. The superfluid to Mott insulator transition and later single-site imaging showed controllable quantum matter. The work is conceptually clear and has shaped how correlated quantum systems are studied.
assessment.attribution: Jaksch and Zoller's proposal and Greiner, Mandel, Hansch and Bloch's 2002 experiment are decisive. Bloch led microscope and many-body developments. Esslinger's Fermi-Hubbard work is also important. The supplied credit permits a fair three-person prize, though the choice among four strong names is hard and I would flag it as unresolved.
assessment.maturity: Mature and widely reproduced across many labs and species. Recognition is timely. Some chance of overlap with the 2001 BEC and 2012 prizes in how the committee views novelty, but the many-body simulation theme is distinct.
uncertainties: Allocation between Bloch, Greiner, Zoller and Esslinger is contested.
Some of the proposed 'quantum simulator' goals (for example, solving open problems in high-Tc physics) are not yet delivered.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Superconductivity and correlated insulators at the magic angle revealed a completely unexpected platform where flat bands from a moire pattern produce strong correlations. This is a new and tunable arena for quantum matter and has generated a large field.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald's 2011 flat-band prediction and the 2018 experiments from Jarillo-Herrero's group are the clear core. Bistritzer is the first author of the theory paper, so exclusion of him is a real attribution cost. Other groups (Dean, Young, Yazdani, Efetov) and the Cao-led experiments complicate it.
assessment.maturity: Replicated in many labs, but the origin of superconductivity and the correlated states is still debated. This makes the interpretation less settled than for the other candidates, so recognition may be somewhat early.
uncertainties: Allocation of credit between Bistritzer and MacDonald, and among experimental groups.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Matter-wave interferometry with atoms is a direct demonstration of quantum mechanics with massive particles and a very sensitive inertial and gravitational sensor. It brings answers to how far wave behaviour extends and gives precision measurements of g, G, and the fine-structure constant.
assessment.attribution: Pritchard's early atom interferometers with gratings, Bordé's theory and Ramsey-Bordé interferometer, and Kasevich and Chu's light-pulse interferometer are separate strands; the supplied three names cover them fairly. Chu has already received the 1997 prize for cooling, which complicates credit, and Chu is not in the credited names.
assessment.maturity: Well confirmed in many labs, with applications in metrology. Possibly the field is still improving in sensitivity, but the principle is mature.
uncertainties: The committee may view this as an extension of earlier prizes (laser cooling 1997, BEC 2001).
Credit among Pritchard, Bordé, Kasevich, Chu and Mlynek is dispersed.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Higgs boson discovery by ATLAS and CMS at the LHC closed the Standard Model and verified the mechanism whose prediction was recognised in 2013. The experiment is a technological and scientific achievement of the first rank. I defer to my particle-physics colleagues for the physics detail.
assessment.attribution: The 2013 prize went to the theorists. Collaborations of thousands make individual attribution hard. Gianotti and Virdee led ATLAS and CMS at discovery, and Evans led the LHC construction. Jenni and Della Negra were founding spokespersons and equally defensible. The Nobel statutes' limit of three makes a fair configuration contested.
assessment.maturity: Fully confirmed, with couplings measured further. The timing is mature, a decade after discovery.
uncertainties: Attribution is difficult in huge collaborations and an institutional-style prize is not possible.
Whether the committee has an appetite for a machine/experiment prize.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The prediction and the observation of the quantum spin Hall state introduced topological insulators, a new classification of electronic states of matter based on bulk topology and protected edge states. It is a fundamental conceptual step beyond Landau and a basis for later work.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the key theoretical proposals. The HgTe prediction by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and the 2007 observation by Molenkamp's group is an important experimental link. Others (Zhang, Fu, Hasan, Moore) also matter, and credit is contested.
assessment.maturity: Reasonably mature, with many materials. Applications remain limited and some of the more extravagant expectations (Majorana, spintronics) have not materialised, but the concepts are well confirmed.
uncertainties: Fair allocation among Kane, Mele, Zhang, Bernevig and others.
Overlap with the 2016 prize (Haldane, Kosterlitz, Thouless).

assessment.nobel_worthiness: IceCube's observation of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos opened neutrino astronomy and later linked them to a blazar and the Galactic plane. This is a new window on the universe from a cubic-kilometre detector in ice. I defer to colleagues on astroparticle details.
assessment.attribution: Halzen was the driving force behind IceCube. Karle and Spiering were important in the detector and the early AMANDA work, but the collaboration is very large, so the choice is not clean.
assessment.maturity: The diffuse flux is well established, and source identification is still in progress. The prize may be somewhat early for the source physics, though the discovery is firm.
uncertainties: The origin of most neutrinos is unknown.
Attribution within a large collaboration and with AMANDA and Baikal predecessors.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Squeezed states of light, together with the theory of quantum-limited interferometry, beat the standard quantum limit. This is quantum mechanics put to use in the most sensitive instruments, in LIGO and others. It connects directly to my interest in where quantum limits arise.
assessment.attribution: Caves proposed squeezing for interferometers, and Kimble's experiments produced the first squeezing in cavities. Slusher et al. and the Hannover group (Schnabel, Vahlbruch) did the later implementation in GEO600. A fair prize is not obvious; Schnabel is a possible third.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed and now routinely deployed in the gravitational-wave detectors. Recognition is timely, but the gravitational-wave prize (2017) covered the detection and the squeezing has had its main impact as an enabling technique.
uncertainties: Credit among Slusher, Yurke, Caves, Kimble and Schnabel is spread.
Whether the committee sees this as an enabling technique rather than a discovery.
